Ocrevus label dosing (BLA 761053, first licensed 2017-03-28; book approvals row from openFDA): 600 mg IV every 6 months after a split first dose. The book's frexalimab price row notes that Ocrevus maintenance is two infusions a year. A biosimilar carries the reference's dosing

Two book rows. (1) lookup.py demand Ocrevus: CMS Part B 2024, $668,719,044 over 11,764 beneficiaries = $56,845 per beneficiary, the figure the book's frexalimab seed also uses. (2) The per-unit price discount of Amgen's own marketed anti-CD20 biosimilar (lookup.py demand Riabni / Rituxan). In CMS Part B 2024, Riabni (Q5123, 10 mg units) was $92,447,260 over 2,331,225 units = $39.656 per unit. Rituxan (J9312, 10 mg units) was $436,980,635 over 5,729,505 units = $76.268. The ratio is 0.5200. $56,845 x 0.5200 = $29,557
column12: Judgement on the discount comparator and year. Riabni is the closest analogue in the book. It is Amgen's own biosimilar, and like ABP 692 it copies an infused anti-CD20 antibody paid under Part B. The seeds suggested for Pavblu, Wezlana and Bkemv are empty in this book, and none of the three has a Part B row in drug_demand. 2024 is Riabni's fourth full year. Its ratio to Rituxan fell from 0.899 (2021) to 0.655 (2022), 0.561 (2023) and 0.520 (2024), so a flat price at the year-4 level understates the early years. It overstates the late years: Ruxience, the first-wave rituximab biosimilar, was down to 0.264 of Rituxan per unit by 2024. The same test on Amgen's other Part B biosimilars in 2024, per 10 mg unit, gives a range. Avsola against J1745 infliximab is 0.730. Mvasi against Avastin is 0.36, but Avastin's Part B units include intravitreal eye use, so that ratio is not clean. Kanjinti against Herceptin is 0.23. Published erosion points the same way. Qian (AJMC 2024, PMID 39745502) finds the rituximab biosimilars' Part B spending per dosage unit fell 15% to 26% in 2022 alone. Kim et al. (JCO Oncol Pract 2026, PMID 42413074) put bevacizumab biosimilars 52.2% below the originator per administration by 2023. The Ocrevus per-beneficiary figure is 89% of a full patient-year (its beneficiaries take 1.78 infusions against a maintenance two). This follows the house per-beneficiary convention; the frexalimab seed makes the same point

column11: SSA section 1847A(b)(8), as amended by IRA section 11403 (CMS, 'Frequently Asked Questions: Inflation Reduction Act', cms.gov/files/document/biosimilar-faqs.pdf). Medicare pays a qualifying biosimilar its own ASP plus 8% of the REFERENCE product's ASP, not 6% of its own. So the Riabni-derived figure carries an add-on of 8% of Rituxan's ASP. Rituxan's ASP is $76.268 / 1.06 = $71.951 per unit, and 8% of it is $5.756. $5.756 / $39.656 = 0.1452 off the Part B figure
column12: Judgement: this departs from the house 0.056604 for a Part B anchor, on the same principle (take the Part B figure back to ASP, which is already net of discounts). A biosimilar's add-on is set on the reference's ASP, and at about half the reference's price that add-on is a larger share of its own payment. Direction checked: 0.1452 off list, so net is $29,557 x 0.8548 = $25,266 per patient-year. That is 47.1% of Ocrevus's ASP of $53,627. The case against: the house 0.056604 would give a net of $27,884, 10% higher. The 8% add-on runs only for biosimilars first paid by 2027-12-31. A 2029 launch reverts to 6% of the reference ASP, which changes the Part B payment (the list) but not the ASP (the net)

column11: Pardo G et al., Neurology and Therapy 2022;11:337-351 (PMID 35020156, doi:10.1007/s40120-021-00319-3). IBM MarketScan Commercial and Medicare Supplemental, 524 ocrelizumab initiators: 75% persistent at 24 months (no switch and no gap of 60 days or more). 1 - 0.75^(1/2) = 0.134 a year
column12: The biosimilar's patients are ocrelizumab patients, so ocrelizumab's own persistence applies, not the 28.6% ofatumumab figure the frexalimab seed uses. The case for lower: Engmann et al., JMCP 2021 (PMID 33624535, doi:10.18553/jmcp.2021.20413) find 8% of ocrelizumab starters in PharMetrics Plus stop within 12 months and 17% within 18 months (11.7% a year). The case for higher: both studies are Genentech-funded. A biosimilar also loses some patients back to the reference: in oncology, 1.2% switched from a biosimilar to the reference within 12 months (Liu et al., JAMA Oncol 2026, PMID 42658505)

column11: 12-year BPCIA reference product exclusivity (PHS Act 351(k)(7)(A)): a biosimilar licence cannot take effect until 12 years after the reference's first licensure. Ocrevus (BLA 761053) was first licensed 2017-03-28 (book approvals row, openFDA), so 2029-03-28. The book's exclusivities row for asset 563 carries 2029-03-28 as a '12-year statutory floor' computed from the Purple Book licensure date (backend/fetchers/exclusivity_purplebook.py), not as a date the Purple Book publishes. BR&R, 'The Early Outlook for Ocrelizumab Biosimilars', 2025-10-21 (biosimilarsrr.com/2025/10/21/the-early-outlook-for-ocrelizumab-biosimilars/): exclusivity runs through March 2029 and the primary US patent expires after October 2028. NCT06700343 primary completion 2027-04-19, estimated (book trials table)
column12: Judgement on timing. A PK/PD readout in 2027 leaves time to file and be approved before the exclusivity date, so launch is expected in 2029 and 2030 is the first full year. The curve starts in 2030, so any revenue from Q2 to Q4 2029 is left out. The case against: Ocrevus Zunovo (subcutaneous, approved 2024-09-13) carries 2036-09-13 in the book, which is again the computed 12-year floor from its licensure date and not an FDA exclusivity determination, so it may not hold; either way an IV biosimilar cannot substitute for it. Roche can move patients onto it before 2029, and an IV biosimilar cannot substitute for it. Roche's remaining patents are not checked here, and BPCIA litigation could delay entry

The Q2 2026 results release (8-K 0000318154-26-000124) reports the ABP 692 study has completed enrolment, again with no partner. Amgen is lead sponsor of NCT06700343

column11: The reference's own treated share. Ocrevus had 11,764 CMS Part B and 3,085 Part D beneficiaries in 2024 (lookup.py demand Ocrevus), 14,849 in all. That is against the 78,050 CMS 2024 disease-modifying-therapy beneficiaries the frexalimab seed sums across the Part B and D files, so 19.02%. Times the 48.49% of Medicare MS patients on any disease-modifying therapy (Li J, Hutton GJ, Aparasu RR, Multiple Sclerosis Journal 2025, as carried by the frexalimab seed): 9.225%. Applied to 913,925, that is 84,312 US patients on Ocrevus
column12: How the reference's treated share is applied: a biosimilar reaches only patients who would otherwise get ocrelizumab, so the pool is Ocrevus's patients, and penetration is the rate at which they move to ABP 692. Cross-check: Roche's FY2025 US Ocrevus sales of CHF 4,874mm (Roche Finance Information Tool) at USD 1.2152 per CHF is $5,923mm. Divided by a full-year ASP of $65,185 (1,200 mg at $54.32 per mg, from CMS Part B 2024 $668.7mm over 11.61mm 1-mg units, divided by 1.06), that is about 90,900 patient-years, or 9.9% of the pool. The two agree within 8%. Judgement: the Medicare treated share stands in for all payers. Younger, commercially insured patients may be more often on high-efficacy therapy, which argues for higher. Part B and D beneficiaries may overlap, and migration to Ocrevus Zunovo before 2029 would shrink the IV pool; both argue for lower. pool_crowding.py groups indications only through indication_groups, which holds no multiple sclerosis group, so on 'Multiple Sclerosis, Relapsing-Remitting' this asset is the only claimant and is not rationed against frexalimab ('Multiple Sclerosis') or fenebrutinib ('Multiple Sclerosis, Chronic Progressive'). That suits it: its patients are Ocrevus's, not the untreated pool's

column10: share of the eligible pool not yet on ABP 692, captured per year
column11: Measured class uptake: rituximab biosimilars rose to 60% of all rituximab claims paid by Medicare Part B in 2022, four calendar years after the first US entry (Qian J, Am J Manag Care 2024;30(12):e359-e363, PMID 39745502, doi:10.37765/ajmc.2024.89644). Book path around that anchor: Part B reference claims (Rituxan + Rituxan Hycela, lookup.py demand) were 197,044 in 2020, 123,181, 91,689, 79,640 and 74,662 in 2024. Holding the total at the 229,222 that Qian's 60% implies for 2022 gives biosimilar shares of 14.0%, 46.3%, 60.0%, 65.3% and 67.4%. Amgen's slice is a third of that: 4.7%, 15.4%, 20.0%, 21.8%, 22.5%. The engine's own identity (incidence 0, 13.4% discontinuation, logistic ramp) was least-squares fitted to those five years. It gives a peak of 0.078, with RMSE 1.9 points, and an engine path of 6.8%, 13.2%, 18.1%, 21.9%, 24.6% of the pool
column12: Judgements, three. (1) One third: three developers run comparative trials against Ocrevus. They are Amgen (NCT06700343), Sandoz (CYB704, NCT06847724; Pearce IP 2025-08-07) and Celltrion (CT-P53, Phase 3; Pearce IP 2023-05-15). Teva/Polpharma and Samsung Bioepis (added January 2026; Pearce IP 2026-01-14) are earlier, and Biocad is Russia-only. Entry order decides the slice. In rituximab, Amgen's third-to-market Riabni held about 5% of biosimilar Part B claims in 2022 (6,988 of the 137,534 implied by Qian), against 49% for Ruxience and about 46% for Truxima by residual. That is the case for lower. The case for higher is Amgen's April 2027 readout, which may put it in the first wave. (2) The class path assumes total rituximab Part B claims held flat from 2020 to 2024, and that Qian's 'all rituximab products' includes Rituxan Hycela. A subcutaneous reference that an IV biosimilar cannot replace is the Zunovo analogue. (3) After year 5 the engine keeps capturing, to a 28.9% share of the pool in year 9, above the measured plateau of 22.5%. Meanwhile the zero-incidence pool leaves out new ocrelizumab starts, so the stock falls to 25% by year 15. These two errors pull in opposite directions. Cross-check: Liu et al. (JAMA Oncol 2026, PMID 42658505) find the reference biologics' Medicare Part B market share fell 31.5% a year after biosimilar entry across bevacizumab, rituximab and trastuzumab. That is a 67.9% biosimilar share by year 3, in line with the path above

column11: same least-squares fit as penetration_peak_pct: the engine's identity against Amgen's one-third slice of the rituximab biosimilar Part B share path, 2020 to 2024
column12: The fit puts year-one capture at 88% of peak, so a biosimilar's uptake is close to a step. It behaves like a formulary switch at loss of exclusivity, not a brand launch. The error surface is flat along this ridge: k 9.7 with midpoint -0.2 fits the same. A ramp forced to start at half-peak (midpoint 0) needs a peak of 0.086 and fits worse (RMSE 2.3 points). The book's MS brand curve (Kesimpta, k 0.735, midpoint 3.62) would badly understate a biosimilar's first three years
